Your first 12 weeks of rucking

Build a routine you can keep. Start with short walks and finish with a longer outing if you are ready.

12 weeks · 3 training days · beginner · Updated 2026-11-24

Who this is for

Start here if you can walk for 20–30 minutes comfortably without a pack. Use no added weight or a light, familiar load. If that walk is not comfortable, begin with shorter walks and repeat the first week as needed.

A normal training week

Tuesday: easy walk or ruck. Thursday: strength (20–25 minutes). Saturday: longer easy outing. Rest or walk gently on the other days. For strength, use 2 sets of 6–10 sit-to-stands, hinges, low step-ups, wall or incline push-ups and light carries; stop with a few repetitions left.

Week by week

  1. 1: Tue 20 min; Sat 30 min; learn pack fit.
  2. 2: Tue 25 min; Sat 35 min; same load.
  3. 3: Tue 25 min; Sat 40 min; try a familiar loop.
  4. 4: Tue 20 min; Sat 30 min; easier week.
  5. 5: Tue 30 min; Sat 45 min; keep the pace conversational.
  6. 6: Tue 30 min; Sat 50 min; practise a drink stop.
  7. 7: Tue 35 min; Sat 55 min; keep load unchanged.
  8. 8: Tue 25 min; Sat 40 min; easier week.
  9. 9: Tue 35 min; Sat 60 min; include a gentle hill if comfortable, or stay flat.
  10. 10: Tue 40 min; Sat 65 min; check footwear.
  11. 11: Tue 40 min; Sat 75 min; rehearse a familiar snack and route.
  12. 12: Tue 25 min; Sat 60–75 min at your own pace; compare how it feels with week 1.

How to adjust

If any week leaves you sore enough to change your walking, repeat or shorten it. Do not chase the calendar. Add pack weight only after the current routine feels comfortably repeatable, and shorten the outing when trying a heavier load.

Put it into practice

A future walking festival with shorter options can give the first twelve weeks a purpose. Check the current programme at Sagamarsjen.

Further reading

  • Petersen, A. (2026, January 5). How PATHFINDER training works. PATHFINDER Ruck Training. — Public overview of an independent commercial training approach; these plans are original and are not its paid materials.
  • Orr, R., Pope, R., Lopes, T. J. A., Leyk, D., Blacker, S., Sanz Bustillo-Aguirre, B., & Knapik, J. J. (2021). Soldier load carriage, injuries, rehabilitation and physical conditioning: An international approach. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 18(8), 4010. — Background reading on load carriage, strength, aerobic work and progression; military workloads are not civilian prescriptions.
